analytic.title: Work In Progress: Best-case response time analysis for Ethernet AVB

div.p: In the automotive industry, Ethernet is currently being introduced as a viable solution for real-time communication with high bandwidth requirements. In this paper, we present and prove a tight bound for the relative best-case response time of a frame in an Ethernet AVB switch compared to its response time in a schedule without interference. Our analysis is based on the observation that frames in a burst, scheduled using a credit shaping policy, may be scheduled earlier in case of interference than in a schedule without interference. We show how an upper bound on the build up of credit may be used to bound this relative speed-up of frames.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the past years, there has been an increase in the number of embedded applications requiring high bandwidth communication and real-time guarantees. In the automotive industry, Ethernet has arisen as a viable solution to meet such demands due to the high bandwidth that it presents. The Ethernet AVB standard and the Ethernet TSN standard that is currently being developed on top of it allow to transport high-volume data with low latency guarantees. In order to meet such real-time requirements, these standards use a nonpreemptive priority scheduling policy. More precisely, the transmission of frames is first distributed over output queues and then scheduled based on their priorities (see Figure 1). The worst-case response time for an Ethernet AVB switch has been extensively studied in the literature, and work on the Ethernet TSN standard is currently in progress. Most of this work is based on busy periods, see e.g. [1][2] [3], but in [4] an alternative approach is suggested, which is independent of the knowledge of the traffic of frames with different priority. In this approach, one assumes to be able to bound the response time in the absence of interference and calculates the worst-case interference in isolation.

Next to worst-case analysis, best-case response time analysis becomes important whenever timing constraints impose lower bounds on response times to events. For example, an airbag has to be inflated neither too earlier nor too late. Also, in the worst-case analysis of multi-hop networks, jitter plays a role, requiring a complementary best-case analysis. To the best of our knowledge, no research has been conducted yet regarding best-case analysis of Ethernet AVB and Ethernet TSN, and certainly not using the relative response-time analysis approach of [4]. In this paper, we make a start, by showing how a relative best-case response time analysis can be performed for Ethernet AVB.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The system model is the same as the one presented in [4]. We are modeling the behavior of a switch that is part of an Ethernet AVB network. The purpose of this switch is the routing of frames from its inputs to its outputs. We are interested in the time it takes to perform such a routing.

In the Ethernet AVB standard, frames are transmitted using non-preemptive static priority scheduling. Frames are gathered in a queue for each priority class and transmitted in order of arrival (FIFO). Furthermore, a frame can only start if there is no higher priority queue that can start (static priority), and if there is no other transmission taking place (non-preemptive). This is illustrated in Figure 1. Ethernet AVB also uses a credit-based shaping mechanism to limit traffic bursts. A credit is assigned to each priority class working with this mechanism. If the credit is nonnegative, a frame may transmit assuming that the other rules for non-preemptive static scheduling also allow this. On the other hand, whenever the credit is negative, lower priority classes are allowed to transmit. Initially, the credit of a priority class X starts at zero and it drops at a rate α - X when a frame is in transmission. When the credit is negative, other frames in the priority class are not allowed to transmit and credit is recovered at a rate α + X . In addition, whenever a priority class has pending frames but cannot transmit, the credit rises at a rate α + X . Finally, positive credit is reset to zero when there are no frames in the queue. Figure 2 illustrates an example of credit-shaping.

Assuming a total bandwidth BW , the Ethernet AVB standard imposes the condition that 0 < α + X < BW for the bandwidth reserved to class X. Furthermore, α - X = BW -α + X is set to the remaining bandwidth. We now present some notation related to the model as described in [4]. For a frame x, we write a(x) and s(x) ≥ a(x) to denote its arrival time and transmission start-time, respectively. Furthermore, C(x) refers to the duration of the transmission of x. All the frames in a class X are assumed to have the same priority. We write C max X and C min X to denote the maximum and minimum frame size in a priority class X respectively. The credit at time t associated with a class X is denoted by CR X (t). The credit evolves according to the rules of the shaper. Furthermore, we call a frame x pending at time t when a(x) ≤ t and s(x) + C(x) > t. The pending load P L X (t) of a priority class X is positive whenever there is a frame of class X pending. Otherwise, P L X (t) = 0.
Finally, an active interval of a priority class X is defined as the time interval [t s , t e ) such that the following holds:
div.formula: • P L X (t s ) = 0 ∧ CR X (t s ) = 0, • P L X (t e ) = 0 ∧ CR X (t e ) = 0, • P L X (t) > 0 ∨ CR X (t) < 0 for all t ∈ (t s , t e ).
div.p: A burst of frames is then defined as the sequence of frames of the same class that arrive in the same active interval.

div.p: Note that the relative bound given in ( 1) is tight whenever the previous frame m 0 before the burst in an un-interfered schedule has a minimum frame size and is sufficiently close to the start of the burst to allow the building up of credit.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we presented and proved the relative bestcase response time of a frame in an Ethernet AVB switch compared to its response time in a schedule without interference. In particular, we showed that frames in a burst in an uninterfered schedule can be scheduled earlier in an interfered schedule when experiencing positive credit at the start of the burst. This positive credit at the beginning of the burst allows some packets to be scheduled continuously without recovery time. Hence, leading to a relative speed-up of frames.
